title: Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record
description: Reform UK has received a second £36m donation in as many days, as cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne matched a record-breaking donation anno
body: Reform UK has received a second £36m donation in as many days, as cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne matched a record-breaking donation announced late on Friday.Thailand-based Harborne wrote in the Telegraph, external that his "competitive spirit" inspired him to equal Ben Delo's donation - the largest ever given to a UK political party - adding he expected "nothing personally" in return.Reform said the £72m would be used to hire "the brightest and best minds to work on policy and the most comprehensive plan for government ever".The party is facing scrutiny over its finances, as the government seeks to cap donations to UK political parties from British expats.There have also been renewed calls by MPs from other political parties for donations from individuals to be capped.The £72m from the two donations is more than the total received by all UK political parties last year, which stood at just over £69m. Reform leader Nigel Farage said Harborne and Delo's "generosity" meant the party would "now be able to fight and win the next general election on a level playing field".A Reform UK spokesman added: "We will now also be able to hire up to 400 campaign managers in every target constituency. We are now on election footing."Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme on Saturday, the party's deputy leader Richard Tice denied accusations the donations were bad for democracy."It's the opposite actually, we're delighted and very humbled by the confidence expressed by two very successful entrepreneurs who realise Britain's in serious trouble," he said."To have that support, to know we can focus on employing the best people, whether it be on social media, policy, campaign managers, that's a good thing."Earlier, speaking to Sky News, Tice said Delo's donation had been an upfront sum "so that the Labour Party can't legislate against it" and would be spent over two or three years.Harborne has already donated millions to Reform and Farage, who is currently under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a £5m cash gift from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.Farage has argued that he was under no obligation to register the "purely private" gift, as it was unrelated to his parliamentary or political activities.The party is also facing scrutiny after a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week showed two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations. The Metropolitan Police has said it is investigating, while the party denies any wrongdoing.The force is also looking into donations given to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell, as well as a company controlled by Tice.Harborne wrote on Saturday that he had "already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life", while Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage"."A start-up party needs more money than can be provided by membership fees alone, to build and sustain itself and be ready for government," he said.Harborne and Delo's donations mark the largest sums received by a UK political party since they had to begin declaring them in 2001.Delo, who also announced his donation in a Telegraph op-ed, said he was giving the money away because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field". He said in April he was moving back to Britain from Hong Kong.Addressing the recent scrutiny of Reform's finances, he said: "My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."Last year, he was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMEX, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.However, the Labour government has introduced a £100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, and plans to introduce a similar one for those who have recently returned to the UK.There were nine donations of £1m or more to political parties in 2025. The largest was £9m given to Reform UK by Harborne.Labour had five donations of £1m or more - totalling nearly £10m - and the Conservatives had three of £1m each.Labour said Reform and Farage still had "serious questions" to answer about their finances.Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said Reform were "drowning" in "sleaze and scandal".She added: "It's time Farage and Reform came clean with the public, fully co-operated with the ongoing police investigations and prove they're not just in it for themselves."Rachel Millward, deputy leader of the Green Party, told BBC News it wanted a cap on donations from individuals of £500,000.She said the donations to Reform were "absolutely staggering amounts", adding:  "What I am very frustrated about is the influence of extreme wealth and the super rich. What I want to see is people in politics representing the needs of their communities and ordinary people."Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for the government to introduce emergency legislation to cap donations.She said: "These are eye-watering amounts of money. This is real emergency for our democracy. It presents a very clear and present threat."Labour MP Stella Creasy and other backbenchers had proposed an amendment to the Government's Representation of the People Bill that would stop donors giving parties over £100,000 a year.But the amendment was never debated in the Commons after the government said it would set up a task force to investigate the issue. The bill will be debated in the House of Lords on Monday.Duncan Hames, Director of Policy and Programmes at campaigning charity Transparency International UK, said: "This is a watershed moment, with two billionaires pledging £72m to one political party in less than 48 hours."This situation is now completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast."

title: Tottenham 0-0 Everton: Spurs blanked again as new era turns into a false dawn
description: The banner held aloft by a Tottenham Hotspur supporter before kick-off was not so much a plea for action as a cry for help."Please Score A Goal" was t
body: The banner held aloft by a Tottenham Hotspur supporter before kick-off was not so much a plea for action as a cry for help."Please Score A Goal" was the message brandished in the direction of the Spurs players as they came out against Everton in search of their first in the Premier League this season.After another goalless 45 minutes, there was a compelling case for a hasty rewrite asking "Please Have A Shot" as, for all their possession, Roberto de Zerbi's expensively assembled side struggled to get anywhere near Jordan Pickford's goal.And so it went on in an increasingly angry and frustrated atmosphere inside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium as Spurs' goalless league streak extended to 407 minutes as a stuttering start to what was meant to be brave new era continued.It was the first time they have failed to score in their opening four league games across all four tiers - and also in four successive Premier League matches since September 2006.The grim statistic would be bad enough in any circumstances, but it is even worse after Spurs spent in excess of £300m in the summer, much of it designed to give De Zerbi's side an added edge.Instead, they are a blunt instrument.This was the first Premier League goalless draw, in the 140th game, at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. On this evidence, there will be more.It may seem early days for an apology to the supporters, but De Zerbi felt the need as he said: "I'm sorry to the fans. We are sorry to the fans."They were fantastic, especially in the first part of the game because when they see the team is playing well, pushing to find the solution they were inside the pitch with my players. Then the reaction of the fans is normal. We have to say thanks all the time to them."Everton could have actually made matters worse, but they are also short of attacking threat themselves - luckily for Spurs.As the second half wore on, the resilient visitors actually missed the game's two best chances through Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Brennan Johnson, while the mood became increasingly sour as nerves and anxiety grew.When £85m summer signing Mateus Fernandes had Spurs' first shot on target after 46 minutes, the stadium rattled to the sound of ironic applause.There was no irony when they played the ball around at the back with only seven minutes left, and when the final whistle sounded it was just like old times - or at least like last season - as jeers sent De Zerbi's players on their way.He went through the card in an attempt to change this embarrassing barren sequence in front of goal, playing new signings from Manchester City, Omar Marmoush and Savio, in the attacking positions, with Dominic Solanke handed his first league start of the campaign.As time went on and the tension mounted, Mohammed Kudus and James Maddison were sent on, but it was another substitute, Lucas Bergvall, who almost snatched victory with a late long-range effort, saved by Everton goalkeeper Pickford after he had gifted the Swede possession and an opportunity.Watching it all from close quarters was a grim-faced Richarlison, the 29-year-old Brazil striker in dispute with the club over the remaining nine months of his contract.He was left out of De Zerbi's Premier League squad after a proposed deadline-day return to former club Everton collapsed. A switch back to Brazil with Vasco da Gama has also failed to materialise.The 'xG' - expected goals - statistic suggests Spurs should have scored three or four goals this season, but their non-penalty xG per shot this season is just 0.066. It gives them an expected conversion rate of 6.6%.In layman's terms, it means they are not very good when comes to creating an attacking threat.De Zerbi, never someone to disguise his emotions, grew more animated and irritated as the game went on, marching on to the pitch at the final whistle for an exchange with substitute Mathys Tel.When any side embarks on the sort of root and branch revolution the Italian presided over this summer, it is inevitable there will be teething problems and time required for understandings and relationships to form.And the change is understandable after two successive 17th-placed finishes in the Premier League. Indeed, Spurs' last league goal actually came against Everton on the final day of last season, courtesy of Joao Palhinha.It kept them in the top flight, allowing them to make a fresh start for this campaign.De Zerbi, who still has much work to do to rid Spurs of the aftershock of two poor seasons, said: "I think in the first 30 minutes we were very, good but we didn't find a goal. I think in that moment we suffer too much with confidence and this is another important part for us at the moment."In the second half, I observed many players had a little less confidence and I don't like this. They have to be happy and understand we are in the right way."The players are human and they have emotions and they think with their head. My position is to help them and stay focus on the improvement we have to do. If we play 90 minutes like we did in the first 30 minutes, I think we are going to win many games."Spurs, however, have a toothlessness that must be a concern. It is certainly one for the supporters who watched their players either take too long over chances or, on many occasions, passed on the responsibility.They also ran into a rugged Everton defence, with Jarrad Branthwaite magnificent as he stepped up his claims for a place in Thomas Tuchel's next England squad after injury troubles.For Spurs, however, there were few positives as the wait for a first Premier League win - and goal - this season goes on.

title: US Open 2026 results: Elena Rybakina beats Aryna Sabalenka to win New York title
description: Elena Rybakina demonstrated why she is the best women's player in the world by beating two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka to win her first US
body: Elena Rybakina demonstrated why she is the best women's player in the world by beating two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka to win her first US Open title.Kazakhstan's Rybakina already knew she would be the new world number one after Saturday's final regardless of the result, and she celebrated with a 6-4 5-7 6-2 victory over the player she will replace.Rybakina was the more composed of the two throughout as she claimed the third Grand Slam title of her career, having triumphed at Wimbledon in 2022 and the Australian Open earlier this year.Sabalenka hoped to soften the blow of losing the top ranking by winning a third consecutive US Open title - but looked fraught in a tense performance.Rybakina and Sabalenka have developed a strong rivalry built not only on their outstanding talent but their contrasting personalities.And Rybakina's ice-cool composure - the direct opposite of the Belarusian's combustible nature - was a key difference as she took control at Flushing Meadows.Rybakina stayed calm in an opening set where her first serve let her down and, despite her biggest weapon not firing on all cylinders, was able to execute a devastating returning game which left Sabalenka frustrated.Sabalenka's groundstrokes improved as Rybakina's level dropped slightly in a tighter second set, taking her third opportunity to force a decider when she swarmed over Rybakina's second serve in the 12th game.But the loose shots from Sabalenka reappeared in the third set - as did the negativity. Rybakina's deep returning pinned Sabalenka to the baseline as she broke for a 2-1 lead, which allowed the incoming world number one to grow in stature.There was a sign of nerves when Rybakina produced a double fault on her first championship point, but she reset admirably to hammer down an ace and underline her status as the best player in the world.Rybakina rarely shows emotion on the court but there was a brief flash of a smile as she clinched her second major victory of an outstanding 2026 season.That illustrated the sense of satisfaction she felt after winning a title few had predicted - not only because she had never previously gone beyond the last 16 in New York but the circumstances coming into the final major of the season.With her penetrating serve and thunderous groundstrokes, Rybakina has a brand of first-strike tennis that can take the racquet out of anyone's hands.Therefore it has been a surprise she has not enjoyed greater success on the Flushing Meadows hard courts, perhaps a result of her personality not being particularly suited to the brash nature of New York."I was coming here for the last 10 years and it was never successful. I'm falling in love with New York more and more," Rybakina, 27, said.What makes the second seed's victory even more remarkable is that she was unsure if she would be fit enough to even play.Rybakina was unable to walk for several days after injuring her ankle in the Cincinnati Open quarter-finals, putting her chances of competing here in serious jeopardy.Not only was Rybakina able to play, but she cruised through her opening four matches thanks to a huge service game that rarely allowed opponents to get into points.Rybakina's next two wins over China's Zheng Qinwen and home favourite Coco Gauff required more work after losing the first sets, proving she had the durability to come through tough battles.Against Sabalenka, she showed both facets of her game, bullying her from the baseline and digging in when necessary to leave her only a French Open title away from the career Grand Slam."Some magic is happening. I was unlucky with injury and just going day by day," Rybakina told Sky Sports."We didn't know how it was going to be so I'm super happy and still can't believe it."The chance to beat the woman who had taken her number one ranking was extra motivation for Sabalenka.However, it was evident from the early stages that the stress of the situation was still troubling the four-time major singles champion - and Rybakina's superb return of serve in the early exchanges only exacerbated it.The pressure Sabalenka was feeling manifested in some aggressive second serves, and it was unsurprising to see one go long for a double fault on the decisive break point in the opening set.While Sabalenka showed the resilience which she has demonstrated in her ascent to the top of the sport, she never looked completely at ease.Dramatic displays of emotion designed to let off steam - yelling, flinging her arms in the air, bouncing her racquet off the court and hiding underneath her towel - were not enough to help produce a gutsy victory which would have ranked among her best.Instead she will have to come to terms with another near miss at a Grand Slam.It was Sabalenka's fifth defeat from nine majors final and provides further weight to the argument that she has underachieved at the biggest tournaments given her dominance on the WTA Tour."The last thing I want to do right now is give a speech but I will try my best," an emotional Sabalenka told the 24,000 crowd on Arthur Ashe Stadium."I wish I could have performed a little bit better, but I guess next year."

title: Chess: 'I was beating adults at chess when I was eight'
description: Image source, Eimear SavageImage caption, Ethan plays for Strand Chess Club in east BelfastByGráinne ConnollyBBC News NI"When I was eight or nine I wa
body: Image source, Eimear SavageImage caption, Ethan plays for Strand Chess Club in east BelfastByGráinne ConnollyBBC News NI"When I was eight or nine I was beating adults at chess and they were raging when they lost, like 'I just lost to a little kid'."Ethan first became interested in chess when he was six years old after he spotted someone else playing.Now 13, he plays for Strand Chess Club in east Belfast and has represented Ireland through all his age groups.Last week he became the youngest Ulster chess champion in history – not just in his age category but across all ages."I was really surprised because I've never won any of the big tournaments before, I've always got so close and I managed to win it in the end," Ethan told BBC News NI.He said his opponents ranged from the ages of 30-65, all at least more than twice his age."That age range is the ages I've been playing against and I didn't get any losses. I got three wins and three draws."Image source, Eimear SavageImage caption, Ethan has represented Ireland in his age groupsEthan said he enjoys the mental challenge of chess."I quite like the thinking part and the opening preparation."The game itself looks really interesting but there is so much more that goes into it before with preparation and tactics."I think I just had a natural ability from the start which I think was quite useful but I think starting at a young age helps quite a lot because it's easier to get it into your brain."I practice a lot and... I'm good at maths. I've got quite a good calculating ability. I think that's probably my main strength."'If you're good enough you're old enough'Image source, Eimear SavageImage caption, Ethan and his mum Eimear who says his success is all down to himselfNeither of Ethan's parents are chess players.However, his mum Eimear Savage said her son was fascinated with the chess board and pieces the moment he first saw them."It was a chance circumstance that Ethan saw someone play chess and thought it looked interesting and he decided he wanted to play and it went from there." She said Ethan's success is all down to himself but his family support him every step of the way."I think Ethan just takes it in his stride and that's him. He enjoys playing chess and he enjoys taking part and when he wins it's a bonus."Ethan has been playing for a while now so people are used to playing against him but maybe when he was younger, I remember he wasn't quite tall enough to see over the table and he had to kneel up on the chair to get a good view of the pieces."That was always a bit of a spectacle but people know him now."Ethan has played as part of the Irish team and has travelled to Paris where he played at the Eiffel Tower, as well as travelling to the Netherlands, Germany and Estonia for tournaments.Tough opponentImage source, family handoutImage caption, Ethan has been beating adult opponents for many years on his way to becoming Ulster championEthan is certainly making a name for himself and his success isn't any surprise to his fellow members at Strand Chess Club.Gareth Annesley said Ethan is a very tough opponent."You wouldn't think he's that young. You think you've got him and he just keeps on playing these moves and it's hard to beat him. He's very resourceful and he's very mature for his age."Even though he's only 13 he's been around for several years, so he has more or less beaten most of the top players in Ulster, so it wasn't a complete shock."If you're good enough, you're old enough in chess really."So what's next for Ethan?"I'm going to keep this up for the rest of my life."My next goal is probably to be Irish champion and then grand master probably. That's the main goal."

schema.headline: Chess: 'I was beating adults at chess when I was eight'

title: Spanish Grand Prix: Lando Norris has real opportunity after coming from nowhere with 'masterpiece' lap
description: It says everything about the remarkable lap with which Lando Norris took pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix that it was a toss-up as to which wa
body: It says everything about the remarkable lap with which Lando Norris took pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix that it was a toss-up as to which was the most important and impressive of two striking statistics.Was it that Norris had improved by a stunning 0.701 seconds between his two laps in final qualifying, to come from nowhere to take a pole that had not looked to be a possibility to McLaren?Or was it that in beating runaway championship leader Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes by 0.011 seconds, Norris had made a mistake at the final corner that cost him more than 0.3secs?McLaren team principal Andrea Stella described Norris' performance as "a masterpiece" and "one of the most impressive laps that I witnessed as somebody that watches telemetry in 450 grands prix, because we were not honestly performing to the level of scoring pole position".As Stella is someone who has worked with Michael Schumacher and Fernando Alonso, his comments carry weight.Norris said: "Most tracks, you know what is perfect, what you really want to achieve in a perfect lap. A very good day is when you get pretty close to that."Until the last corner, I think I matched that perfection level in pretty much every corner."So, yeah, it's a dream to achieve a lap like that. So it was easily one of the best laps I've ever done."Everything came together perfectly. I got the timing of everything so dialled in, with the kerb hits, how you hit the kerb, brake points, all of these things. It's so easy to make a mistake on a day like today and a track like this, but really I just got it right on the most important lap I had to do."So, very excited, very pleased and it's not often you achieve a lap like today and it's a pretty awesome feeling when you do."That last corner, Norris said, "I thought I was in the wall and that was just from over-pushing. I got a bit excited in the car and I just over-pushed the entry."Stella said: "The most impressive thing is the fact that it's a pole position despite having lost 0.35secs in the last corner, which means that it would have been a pretty convincing pole position without this issue."The thing that makes the lap unique when you look especially at the telemetry is the precision - the braking, the speed you carry in entry, the striking of the kerbs, the going on power. Everything is executed with a pretty unique level of precision."Norris does not use a display on his dashboard showing his progress compared with his previous lap, the so-called delta, as most other drivers do."I don't need my delta," he said. "I can feel when I do what I need to do and when I get a good exit, when I'm on the limit of things. When I'm kind of a bit uncomfortable in corners is normally when it's going pretty well. So, I could feel it and I feel like I just made all the right things. My feet were doing what I wanted, and that's normally when things are going well."Antonelli expecting cautious first 10 laps with high degradation expectedThe new Madring street circuit is in an unprepossessing location, snaking around an exhibition centre near the Spanish capital's international airport, about a 15-minute drive from the city with no traffic.But as a test for the drivers, it is right up there."Very high risk" and "less margin than Monaco" were two remarks made by Mercedes driver George Russell over the weekend.The walls are close and the demands of the circuit are amplified by the fact that the barriers angle back towards the track on the exit of many corners, making it all too easy to hit them.Despite that, qualifying ran incident-free, which was very much not the prediction, especially after there were two red flags in final practice earlier in the day, one caused by seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, the other by Haas driver Oliver Bearman.Whether the race goes the same way is an altogether different matter.This was Norris' third pole of the year, and after the first two he took dominant wins in Hungary and the Netherlands.At those races, though, McLaren were in a very different place."Tomorrow is going to be a very tough day," Norris said. "It's not going to be as straightforward as in Zandvoort and Budapest. There we were the quickest car. Yes, I'm on pole now, but we're not in the quickest car. It took a perfect lap to get me on pole by 0.011secs today."Norris, it's worth saying, also took pole despite missing virtually all of second practice with a gearbox problem.Not only does that make the achievement all the more impressive, it also means he missed out on potentially crucial information about race-distance running, as that session is when the teams do their race simulations.Tyre degradation is expected to be high. The high-grip, smooth new track surface, combined with the longest pit lane of the year - Norris jokingly described it as "6km long", cut in half as it is by a building - should in theory lead to a one-stop strategy.But the high tyre degradation could well push it to a two-stop, and because teams will try to avoid that, Antonelli said, "probably is going to be grandmother driving in the first 10 laps - we saw how steep the degradation can be, especially if you push too early".In Norris' favour is that overtaking is expected to be especially difficult.The straights are short, and some of the corner entries, which combine braking and turning, mean, as Verstappen put it, "there are no corners where you can pass".The drivers generally liked the challenge of the new track, Norris described it as "a little bit of everything".But all agreed on the fact that the corner entries need to be changed to facilitate racing.Verstappen, who qualified third, said: "You can't overtake. So, in some places, the braking zones, like, they need to learn that it should never be that you have to steer, that you have to combine under braking, because it doesn't allow any kind of overtaking."Antonelli said: "It's going to be tight. I spent two laps behind the Williams, trying to painfully get past. But it's just really difficult."And when you're behind, it's tough. Yeah, the only thing you can do is try to put pressure on the car in front, trying to make them do mistakes or make them deg a bit more."The difficulty in overtaking is what makes this a real opportunity for Norris to take a third win of the season, even if the McLaren is not the fastest car.As he put it: "It's a long race, it's a new track. You've got to know what corners to push, what corners not to push, all of these different things, what the battery's then going to do."There's a lot of stuff that I've got to spend my time doing tonight. So, it's probably going to be a late one to try and get ahead of the game in some sorts. But the main part of the job was done today, so that's the bit I'm most happy about."

schema.headline: Spanish Grand Prix: Lando Norris has real opportunity after coming from nowhere with 'masterpiece' lap

title: Critics celebrate Céline Dion's 'risky' comeback show in Paris
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByGrace Eliza GoodwinIconic Canadian pop singer Céline Dion has kicked off her long-awaited comeback show in Paris on Saturd
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByGrace Eliza GoodwinIconic Canadian pop singer Céline Dion has kicked off her long-awaited comeback show in Paris on Saturday, after a six-year hiatus due to health issues.The 58-year-old superstar was diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder called stiff person syndrome in 2022, which forced her to pull back from touring. Dion, one of the best-selling musical artists of all time, has not performed a full show since a 2020 concert in New Jersey - the last before the Covid pandemic cut her tour short. In 2024, she performed just one song at the Paris Olympics closing ceremony.Saturday marked the first of Dion's 26-show residency at the Paris La Défense Arena, Europe's largest covered concert arena."I made a promise," she told the Paris audience of about 30,000 people in her emotional return."I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage. And here I am. Singing for you, and singing for me," she said."I am everything I am because you loved me," she told the crowd.She also broke down in tears after finishing a song, telling the audience: "I had promised myself not to cry." "But I'm so happy to see you all. I missed you."They weren't the only tears of the night, as the star appeared to be overcome with emotion several times.Dion will be performing in Paris throughout September and October and into the New Year. Figure caption, Watch: Celine Dion fans prepare for much-anticipated comeback concert in ParisThe Mirror's Lucy Needham, external noted that the singer was 50 minutes late to start, and may have needed extra time to "compose herself" for the "emotionally charged return"."Eyes-brimming, the veteran singer gave herself little nods of approval after every line, before finally breaking down at the end of the track, seemingly overwhelmed at having made it through."After beginning her set in a black gown, she later changed into a trouser suit "to show off some of those signature kooky dance moves," says Needham, adding that she appeared "to be having the time of her life, gyrating and slapping her thighs with glee".The night was a "a tense, tearful, joyous affair probably even more so for the singer than for her loyal audience," writes The Telegraph's Neil McCormick, external.She started out slow, he says. "Her voice sounded fragile and exposed, but at least it was her distinctive voice, not some autotuned approximation.""At first, she was clearly struggling to hold herself together," he continues. "Her vocals wobbled dangerously, as if about to crack or collapse. But she was gaining confidence with every moment back on stage."She broke down in tears as the audience roared in approval after the first song, and addressed the crowd in both French and English during the set. "This was a high-stakes, high-wire return, perhaps the riskiest comeback in the history of showbusiness," McCormick continues, referring to her health condition. But he concludes: "I honestly think I prefer this less superhuman Céline. Her voice is still great, but a bit more raw and real, with a rougher tone, less smoothness in the runs and more edge to her whoops and shrieks."Image source, Getty ImagesSarah Leavitt, reporting from Paris for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), external, said the crowd "was left without words" by the stunning performance.She noted that she didn't want to cry, but "of course she cried right away."Dion also "endeared herself" to the crowd by saying during one song that she wanted to stop and start over. Will Hodgkinson at the Times of London, external writes in his review, "miraculously, her art will go on," that the performance was "overwhelming".She "looked suitably humbled and tearful" as she emerged, he said, going on to praise the stage direction."Truly, she was throwing the love at the crowd, who threw it right back at her. There was no holding back. It was quite overwhelming, actually," he writes.The performance was "complete with both costume, key change and air of tragic, important romance"."Céline Dion's strength lies in being a diva with the common touch while being as French as they get, even if she is Canadian. She fulfilled that role with all the verve you could hope for," writes Hodgkinson."The concert had a spiritual feel, with visual interludes steeped in biblical imagery alluding to a pilgrimage," Elsa Keslassy writes for Variety., externalIn video clips, Dion is seen wandering in a desert. "The set design was highly cinematic, with a monumental staircase sweeping up one side and a moon dominating the stage, while the backdrop appeared to have a stark, almost brutalist gray texture."The star, known for power ballads like My Heart Will Go On and Because You Loved Me, has said she will not let her diagnosis control her life."The way I see it, I have two choices. Either I train like an athlete and work super hard, or I switch off and it's over," she told French Vogue magazine, external in 2024."I've chosen to work with all my body and soul, from head to toe, with a medical team."Figure caption, Watch: Céline Dion duets with young fan ahead of comeback concertWhen Dion announced the first leg of her Paris residency back in March, nine million fans signed up for early access tickets to the concerts, French outlet FRI reported. The shows sold out so fast that her management company soon announced an additional 10 shows scheduled for May 2027, which have also since sold out. Fans who were unable to snag tickets to one of the highly anticipated shows have not been left out entirely - events honouring Dion's comeback have dominated Paris in recent weeks. Céline Dion tribute boat cruises on Seine - complete with costume contests, sing-alongs, DJ sets, are happening throughout September.Ahead of Saturday's show, fans gathered outside Dion's Paris hotel, LeRoyal Monceau, as early as 06:00 local time to catch a glimpse of the star. Paris City Hall organised a massive karaoke event on Friday night, attended by thousands, to celebrate Dion's return to the stage. "I couldn't get tickets to the concert. I'm still keeping my fingers crossed and hoping, but I thought to myself: at least I can share a moment here with all the fans," Rania, a participant at the event, told Reuters. Earlier this week, thousands of fans also gathered at a historic theatre in central Paris for two nights of karaoke and activities inspired by Dion's music.And Paris venues and night clubs are hosting Dion-themed events around the city on Saturday night for fans who couldn't get tickets to the actual show. Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty Images

schema.headline: Critics celebrate Céline Dion's 'risky' comeback show in Paris

title: Some dentists say more young people are grinding their teeth - are you one of them?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nearly one in four people are thought to have bruxism, although most are unaware they grind their teethByRuth
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nearly one in four people are thought to have bruxism, although most are unaware they grind their teethByRuth CleggHealth and wellbeing reporterElla can't remember when she first started grinding her teeth at night, but she can vividly recall the excruciating jaw ache, the headaches, and being told her molars were disappearing."I was in so much pain," Ella says. "My face was changing shape and my teeth were at risk of breaking - I knew I had to do something about it."The 31-year-old has bruxism, a condition which can cause regular and often intense teeth grinding, but says the treatment she's recently had has "without a doubt" changed her life.Bruxism affects millions like Ella across the UK, external. Some studies suggest nearly one in four people experience the condition, although many may be unaware until symptoms appear.According to the British Dental Association there is some anecdotal evidence that bruxism is becoming more common, but no specific figures. However, some dentists have told the BBC they are worried about the increasing number of young people they're seeing with dental problems caused by incessant gnashing."It is definitely on the rise," Dr Aditi Desai, president of the British Society of Dental Sleep Medicine (BSDSM), says. "And it's no surprise given that life itself nowadays can be so stressful."Image source, EllaImage caption, Ella says constant teeth grinding enlarged her masseter muscles and widened her jaw (pictured, left, before treatment and, right, afterwards)Studies, external suggest many of us Bruxers do it because of stress - but why do our jaws carry the burden of our everyday lives? What can we do about it? And can it actually be a good thing in some cases?Bruxism is an umbrella term which groups together four different jaw movements - clenching, grinding, bracing and thrusting.Some people grind at night, others through the day. Some barely notice they're doing it, while others can gnash through mouthguards and wake even the deepest sleeping bed partners. So how can you tell if you do it? Here are the signs to look out for: Worn, chipped or flattened teethHeadaches or facial pain in the morningJaw stiffnessDisrupted sleep and daytime tirednessIncreased tooth sensitivityEarache or pain near the temples without infectionTeeth grinding is also mentioned more frequently in therapy according to the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy, which says people nowadays are more aware of how their mental health impacts their body.Psychotherapist Rahi Popat says more of his clients - particularly younger ones - say they or someone else have noticed they've been grinding their teeth, "and they can often link that to a really stressful time in their lives and realise that's when their teeth grinding either increased or even started".'A way of releasing some of the stress' Trauma and stress can put you in "fight or flight" mode, where your heart rate increases, you release adrenaline, and your muscles tense, preparing the body for an external threat, he says. And because the jaw and the nervous system are so closely linked through the major cranial nerves, our muscles are triggered and we clench and grind our teeth."If we do it overnight, it's a way of our bodies releasing some of the stress and tension we might have felt through the day," Popat explains.For Ella, nocturnal teeth grinding in her sleep became a way to release tension that had built up while she was awake. "I know it's to do with my stress levels," Ella says. "I have high functioning anxiety - you wouldn't think it if you met me."I'm busy, and I go out a lot to mask it."In her 20s, she says she just "put up" with the pain. But a few years later, when her dentist told her that her teeth were at risk, Ella decided to get treatment.Image source, EllaImage caption, After her dentist injected her jaw muscles with Botox, Ella says her sleep and mental health improvedEven though it's not routinely offered on the NHS, Ella decided to pay her dentist to inject Botox into her masseter muscles - the ones that control her jaw. The procedure relaxed them and reduced the tension in her face, and should last 3 to 4 months."Over the past few months I've been able to sleep properly," she says. "I've got so much more energy in the mornings, the pain has reduced and my face is not as square."Dr Simon Cove, a dentist who treats both private and NHS patients, says the physical impact of grinding on our teeth can be huge.He uses a 3D scanner to assess his patients' teeth, and can see the wear over time."Often people are not even aware they are doing it, but then we get to see the damage," he says. "If the teeth have been worn down to such an extent, treatment can be extremely complex and can cost thousands of pounds."But he says such cases are relatively uncommon and can take years to develop.Image source, Simon CoveImage caption, A 3D scan can reveal the damage that teeth grinders are doing to their teethWhile you can treat the symptoms - by wearing a mouthguard, for example - getting to the source of what's causing your teeth grinding is just as important, says dental sleep specialist, Dr Aditi Desai."Too often," she says, "dentists give out mouthguards without checking why it is happening."It's vital that serious, underlying conditions like obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) are considered, she says. OSA is caused by a blocked airway, so a patient may grind their teeth to move the blockage in order to be able to breathe again."That's a very good example of why bruxism can keep you alive," says Prof Frank Lobbezoo, a leading researcher on the condition.And even though bruxism has its negatives (tooth damage, sleep disruption, jaw ache, to name but a few), it's not always the "bad guy", he explains."Bruxism is also important for the production of saliva," Lobbezoo says. "Moving the jaw muscles activates the big salivary glands. It cleans the mouth, it protects the teeth and it's vital for digestion." Some studies also suggest that chewing can help with cognition."We know this in animals, and our preliminary research is showing it in humans," he says. "By working our jaw muscles we are stimulating blood flow to the brain."But teeth grinding can also cause chronic pain, which can have a huge impact on your daily life.What is the treatment for bruxism? Dentist Riaz Yar, a specialist in prosthodontics, treats patients struggling with the effects of severe bruxism - worn, cracked and fractured teeth, and dental work that keeps failing. Many also arrive with chronic jaw or facial pain and report poor sleep, all of which need assessing in their own right, he says, rather than simply being blamed on the grinding.In the past, Yar says, teeth grinding was considered simply a mechanical problem of the jaw, but now there is strong evidence that it is much more complex. It's a "biopsychosocial issue", he says, driven by the brain and nervous system and shaped by the whole person."We take into account their sleep patterns, their diet, their weight, the amount they exercise, what medication they might be taking and we assess for signs of sleep disorders," he says. "Many factors can contribute to a patient grinding their teeth, so addressing the condition requires a multidisciplinary approach." How best to tackle it? These things might help: Mouthguard to wear at night to protect your teethIf linked to sleep apnoea, devices such as a CPAP machine or a mandibular advancement device (MAD) to help keep the airway openPhysiotherapyTalking therapies such as CBTLifestyle changes to help reduce stress and improve sleep such as exercise, cutting down on alcohol, stopping smoking and eating healthierAlong with muscle-relaxing injections, Ella says she is also meditating to try to reduce her anxiety and free herself from the tension she regularly carries."Having treatment has transformed my life," Ella says, "now I want to try and figure out the root cause."

schema.headline: Some dentists say more young people are grinding their teeth - are you one of them?

title: Liverpool 0-0 Fulham: More dropped points at Anfield - is it too early for Liverpool to worry?
description: Two Premier League matches at Anfield. Two draws. For just the third time in 63 years, Liverpool have failed to win either of their opening home games
body: Two Premier League matches at Anfield. Two draws. For just the third time in 63 years, Liverpool have failed to win either of their opening home games of a league season - not exactly the flying start new boss Andoni Iraola would have been dreaming of.After such an encouraging midweek performance against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League, full of urgency, Saturday's goalless draw against Fulham was a flat follow-up, especially with the Cottagers lacking in confidence and having conceded seven goals in their first three league games.The Reds looked physically and mentally tired and, to put it bluntly, like an entirely different team to the one that won against a Diego Simeone side that made it to the Champions League semi-finals last season. On the first real look at how Iraola's style will cope with two games a week, this was certainly not what the Liverpool head coach, nor the Anfield crowd, would have wanted to see. Former boss Jurgen Klopp would often speak about recognising his team based on their identity and intensity rather than just their colours and judging by Iraola's words since he took over, the Spaniard wants the same too. Iraola said: "What was lacking was quite clear, it is the first game we had problems to create chances and score goals and make the difference offensively, and that is the main reason we couldn't create chances."His side are still unbeaten and it is hardly a crisis, but he will look at a return of six points from their first four Premier League games as disappointing, particularly by dropping four points at home to Nottingham Forest and Fulham, with another draw coming at Newcastle and their sole success at Ipswich.Keeper Alisson told Sky Sports: "We are not happy at all with the draw. It is not something that should happen with Liverpool. To be unbeaten, but with three draws, is not something to celebrate too much with this shirt."If we want to do something special [this season] we have to cope with playing a game Wednesday, Saturday and then Tuesday. "We need to have the right mental state and that was not the case from what we showed. Inside we have it, but we have to just put it out and put more energy on the pitch."The £364m attacking trio of Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz started together for the first time in a league game and although Liverpool had decent chances, they created nowhere near enough. Isak's 16 touches in 90 minutes was the second fewest for an outfield Reds player on record, having had the fewest (14) against Forest a fortnight ago.German Wirtz looked a shadow of the player who was terrific in midweek against Atleti and while Barcola and Isak had a few encouraging moments, that is a partnership that will take time to develop."Bradley is one we are building up physically with games and the games will give him the condition we want," Iraola told Match of the Day."But it is not just Bradley, we lack the freshness. I only remember one clear chance [for Fulham] and we kept the structure but offensively we need to do much better."Before the game against Atletico Madrid, Iraola was asked about how he sought to strike the right balance, with the intensity levels he craves and such a busy schedule.His response was he didn't want his players to save energy because they had another game in three days."You play 55 minutes for me and you are dead and ask for a sub, then perfect," said Iraola. "We have a top-level 55 minutes and then a top-level 35 minutes."By the hour mark against Fulham, all three of Iraola's changes to the starting line-up were replaced, with left-back Kostas Tsimikas taken off at half-time and Ryan Gravenberch and Victor Munoz replaced after 60 minutes.Despite sending on Milos Kerkez, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister, Rio Ngumoha and Jeremie Frimpong, Liverpool showed little improvement.Iraola admitted: "The players were tired and there is a lack of freshness - we cannot hide it. This is the worst turnaround in terms of 60 or 70 hours [since the last game], but this is going to happen in the season and we have to adapt and it is these kind of games that you need to win sometimes with a set-play or a moment of brilliance."It is still early, but already there is a realisation from Iraola and his players that when they have such short turnarounds between games, perhaps it is a case of adapting and finding ways to get a result. With at least seven more Champions League games to follow and a Carabao Cup tie at home to Tottenham on Tuesday, Liverpool must adapt sooner rather than later as the fixture list cranks up if they are to show they can challenge for honours this season.

title: Meena and Minal: Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters
description: Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each ot
body: Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each other in the Netherlands, have now discovered they are biological sisters.Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen, born in the early 1980s, were adopted from two different orphanages in the western Indian city of Mumbai within months of their birth. When they first met in their early teens at an event hosted by the adoption agency their parents had used, they were struck by the uncanny similarities in their appearance and mannerisms.Meena, now 43, remembers the day clearly. "All the adopted children were brought together to hang out and bond and have dinner."Both Meena and Minal were with friends who noticed how similar they looked."They said, 'Look at yourselves in the mirror'. "And I was like, 'Oh my God, she has my nose! We have the same laugh'. "At dinner, I kept looking at her the whole time," Meena told the BBC from her home in the Netherlands.The following day, the girls exchanged telephone numbers and addresses and promised to keep in touch.Even though there was no indication they were related by blood, their connection was instant, and for years they wrote each other letters, often addressing each other as "Sis" because "we felt that way".They wrote about school, friends, boys, going out and dancing. They told each other about the sports they played and discussed music, discovering they both loved Backstreet Boys.Then 15 years ago, they lost contact. Minal had moved to France. And Meena had recently had her first child and got busy.In 2017, Meena attended another meeting of adoptees from India where she heard about DNA testing and decided to take a test herself. But she never found any matches and earlier this year, deleted the app because her phone storage was full. Then on 20 May, Meena received a message from Minal on Facebook."'Remember me?' she asked. Minal had taken a DNA test in April while visiting her parents in the Netherlands and attached a screengrab of her test result."I reinstalled the app. I was so nervous I entered wrong passwords 10 times before I was able to log in," Meena says.The result couldn't have been clearer - the two women were "a 100% match". "I had a 'full sister' which means we shared the same biological mother and father," Meena explains. "It was like I had an adrenalin shot. I cried. Minal was my missing puzzle piece I had waited so long for. We had called each other sister. "This DNA match was the confirmation that all our intuition was right."On a fine sunny day in August the old friends met for the first time since discovering they were sisters. "It was amazing. It felt like homecoming," Meena, now a mother to three children, says. "For years, Minal and I had felt a big hole in our hearts. We feel like we've been completed. Everything now feels like it's supposed to be." Reporting on their "emotional reunion", Reuters said "tears, hugs ​and laughter punctuated their ​meeting... followed by their first selfie together".Minal, 44, who lives in France with her partner and two sons, told the agency that when her ⁠DNA results came in April, she had initially not realised her match was the same teenage girl who had clung to her when ​they first met 30 years ago. It only sank in when she looked at her photos on social media. "'Meena: Sister.' I couldn't believe it. We were friends before we were sisters. "We were sisters the whole time," she said, "but we didn't know." Since May, Meena and Minal have been speaking every other day. They've met each other's spouses, children, brothers and parents."Everyone notices how we finish each other's sentences, how we move our heads or walk similar," Meena says.The fact they are siblings is still sinking in, she says."Sometimes we talk for two hours and lose track of time, suddenly remembering that we have to do groceries or pick up children from school."One thing she and her sister would "love to do", Meena says, is return to the place where it all began."We'd love to go to India together sometime, to walk through the streets of Mumbai together. "There were times when we both felt very lonely, like when I lost my dad or went through a heartbreak," she says."I regret we couldn't be with each other - we could have shared happiness, helped each other in tough times."

schema.headline: Meena and Minal: Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters

title: They lost their jobs after posting about Charlie Kirk, but some have no regrets
description: In September 2025, Gerald Bourguet felt he was finally living his dream life: he and his wife had bought a house with a pool, they had just welcomed a
body: In September 2025, Gerald Bourguet felt he was finally living his dream life: he and his wife had bought a house with a pool, they had just welcomed a baby boy, and he was writing about professional men's basketball as his full-time job.But all of that changed after he made a series of online posts critical of the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk hours after he was fatally shot on 10 September, while speaking on the campus of Utah Valley University.In the posts, Bourguet described Kirk as an "evil man" and suggested he had dedicated his life to hateful causes. He also criticised Kirk's supporters saying they had not been vocal about school shootings."I had seen the way that people were talking about this person - kind of eulogising him and lionising him and it bothered me based on a lot of the things that he had said," Bourguet told the BBC.Kirk, who founded Christian youth organisation Turning Point USA, was a divisive figure in US politics. For many on the political right, he was charismatic and had a unique skill in making conservative ideas appeal to young people. But for his opponents, his comments on a large swathe of issues from race to immigration, gun control and gender identity were deeply offensive.Screenshots of Bourguet's critical posts went viral quickly. He was fired from his job, his address was exposed online, and he began receiving threatening text messages, he said. Concerned for their safety, the family fled the state with their four-month-old. They returned months later to sell the house and permanently relocated.A year later, he says he doesn't regret what he said, but acknowledged: "My life will never be the same after this". "At age 35, I am having to start over in a lot of respects… I wouldn't wish this on my worst enemy," Bourguet said from his new location, which the BBC agreed not to disclose.PHNX Sports, Bourguet's former employer, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.Bourguet was one of hundreds fired or disciplined over critical comments of Kirk after his death. While some of those who have lost their jobs have been reinstated or received restitution - sometimes in the millions - others like Bourguet have had to rebuild from scratch.In the aftermath of Kirk's assassination, most people kept their feelings to themselves, or shared them with close friends.But on polarised social media, people rushed to laude, or denounce, the controversial activist. Some called the criticisms, posted hours after his death, tasteless. But others called for swift action, arguing they were callous, mocking, and could even incite further violence.Laura Loomer, an influential right-wing commentator with nearly 2 million followers on X, warned Kirk's critics to "prepare to have your whole future professional aspirations ruined". The push for punishment also came from the highest levels of US government."When you see someone celebrating Charlie's murder, call them out," Vice-President JD Vance said days after the assassination. "And hell, call their employer," he added.White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told the BBC: "Anyone who engages in or endorses political violence or assassination culture must be condemned in the harshest terms possible."Critics on the left said there was a difference between criticism of Kirk and celebrating his death. Some accused these conservative leaders of hypocrisy, as many had previously bemoaned the rise of "cancel culture" – where people who voice controversial opinions face severe consequences at work and socially."Cancel culture can be good, it's bad when it's applied in the wrong ways," Jordan Pace, a Republican member of the South Carolina House of Representatives, told the BBC. "If you are someone who celebrates political assassinations and the murder of an innocent man with two young children in a way that many people did, then yeah, that's an appropriate way for society to function, to shame those people."Pace had previously called for defunding universities in his state if they didn't take actions against employees who made comments about Kirk. One of his posts was re-shared by US President Donald Trump.Across the nation, some employers – private and public – acted swiftly to the pressure campaign. Reliable figures on the number of people fired or disciplined are hard to come by, but a Reuters tally last November found more than 600 instances. It is likely an under-count because not all cases received national or local press attention.The specific actions that led to these disciplinary decisions run the gamut. In Tennessee, anthropology professor Tamar Shirinian was suspended and later fired for a Facebook comment saying "the world is better off" without Kirk.A Delta Air Lines flight attendant was fired after posting "good riddance" in response to Kirk's killing. Office Depot supply store fired an employee for refusing to serve a customer who had wanted to print flyers for a Kirk vigil. Delta Air Lines declined to comment. Office Depot did not respond to a request for comment.Others were disciplined even if they did not make any direct comments about Kirk or his death. Darren Michael, a theatre professor in Tennessee, was fired after he posted a screenshot of a news article from 2023, that covered Kirk's controversial speech on gun control. In the article, Kirk is quoted saying protecting citizens' rights to own guns was worth it even if it led to some gun deaths every year.Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission fired biologist Brittney Brown after she reposted a meme that also satirised Kirk's position on gun violence in light of his own shooting."I was absolutely gutted," Brown said about her firing to the BBC. "It was like the entire world just completely flipped on its head in a moment."In the year since Kirk's killing, dozens of lawsuits have been filed across the country by people fired for their comments about the activist, arguing their terminations violated their rights to free speech. The suits have led to substantial pay outs in some cases.Brown agreed to a $485,000 (£355,000) financial settlement – about 12 times Brown's annual salary. Darren Michael was reinstated by the Austin Peay State University and in January, the school agreed to pay him $500,000 to settle legal claims. The school did not respond to a request for comment.In the largest settlement reviewed by the BBC, the University of Tennessee agreed to pay $1.9m to resolve a lawsuit brought by anthropologist Tamar Shirinian, over her "better off" comment. As part of the settlement, she will not be reinstated and has agreed not to reapply for future positions at the school.Recently, an arbitrator ordered The Washington Post to rehire, with back pay, opinion journalist Karen Attiah, who was fired for her online posts that said in part she was not going to engage in "performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence".Several other lawsuits remain pending, the BBC found.Most of the legal actions have been pursued by employees of government institutions, or unionised workers, who have some free-speech protections.But in the US, most private sector employees work under "at-will" contracts, which means they can be can be fired without reason.Even those who have scored some victories don't see it as a win."All I wanted was my job back," biologist Brown said. "How much taxpayer money did they waste on this when I barely made $40,000 a year? So no, it does not feel like justice."Shirinian told the BBC she too had wanted to return to her job but felt a legal case could be a lengthy affair."I took a settlement because this allows me to move on with my life," she told the BBC. "The one small regret that I have is that I will not see my day in court and justice will not be served in that way. But I think that the number of the settlement actually speaks to that anyway."The University of Tennessee and Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. As an at-will employee at a private company, Bourguet is unlikely to prevail in a lawsuit challenging his dismissal. A year on, he said he has struggled to find work. The new state he lives in has a professional basketball team, but he believes the ordeal has made him unemployable in the small world of sports writers. Instead, he's started his own podcast, although he doubts he can earn enough through it to pay the bills."I have accepted that that life is over and that I need to start a new one." Leaving the country is now on the table, he said.Despite the huge personal and professional costs, those who spoke to the BBC said after months of reflection, they did not regret their actions."I have a right to say what I want to say," Brown said. "They are the ones who should have the regrets, not me," she said referring to her former employer.Shirinian apologised to the university days after her suspension. She told the BBC her comment was "an emotional outburst" that was not intended to be public and that she regretted the tone used."I don't regret the sentiment, however" she said, adding "the sentiment was that I am not sad. And I refuse to be made to feel like I have to be sad that someone who was so hateful was killed".Bourguet also said he does not regret his comments although he has conflicting thoughts about its consequences."I don't regret that line of thinking because I think it's important to push back on things that are steeped in hatred," he said, referring to Kirk's political message. "I don't regret what I said. I don't regret the way that I said it. I do regret the ripple effects that came from it and the way that they impacted me, my career, my family, and my son."

schema.headline: They lost their jobs after posting about Charlie Kirk, but some have no regrets

title: World's tallest living horse based in Towcester 'still growing'
description: 'He's massive!' Meet Hugo, the world's tallest horseImage source, GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS 2027Image caption, One of Hugo's owners, Lisa Masters, said h
body: 'He's massive!' Meet Hugo, the world's tallest horseImage source, GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS 2027Image caption, One of Hugo's owners, Lisa Masters, said he was "a big softie, like an oversized dog"ByAlex PopeA Shire horse that has entered the record books as the world's tallest living horse could exceed his height as he is still growing, his owner has said. Hugo, who lives in Towcester, Northamptonshire, has already reached an "abnormal" 199cm tall, about 6.5ft, or 19.2 hands, to the withers or ridge at the base of the neck.Guinness World Records said the four-year-old's stature was officially assessed by a vet and he was measured without shoes to ensure an accurate result.Owner Brett Masters said Hugo received "a huge amount of care" from a chiropractor, dentist, vet and masseuse, meaning he lived a "five-star lifestyle".Shire horses are known for their height and their large stature means they are able to pull heavy weight, which is why they have been historically used as working horses on farms and for transport.The tallest and heaviest horse ever documented, external was a Shire gelding named Sampson, who was later renamed Mammoth - bred by Thomas Cleaver of Toddington Mills in Bedfordshire, which stood at 2.19 metres - or 7ft 2.5 in - in 1850.Image source, Tove Valley Shire HorsesImage caption, Hugo has his teeth checked twice a year by his dentist, HannahMasters, from Tove Valley Shire Horses, said the breed was his passion. He was approached by officials from Guinness World Records as Hugo was "locally famous", and they had been told: "There is this really big horse, you need to speak to these guys."Masters said that when he acquired Hugo - at the age of 18 months - he had no idea he was "very tall, abnormally tall"."He's still got three years of growing left, he won't stop until he's about eight and a half, he's only a baby," he said."It will cause issues, so we have to be very careful with him."He has a chiropractor, has regular massages, the dentist visits every six months, and the vet checks him all the time as his growing plates are hyperactive. "He has lots of supplements and a careful feed regime."He lives a five-star lifestyle, he wants for nothing."Image source, GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS 2027Image caption, Brett Masters said when Hugo goes out and about, people stop to admire himMasters added: "Every time he goes out, people stop, they film him, shout at you that 'he's massive'."He's the kindest, most gentle kind of horse."He said he did not receive any form of payment for his official recognition, but joked: "If any carrot farmer wants to give him some carrots, he'd kindly have them." Hugo is kept busy by taking part in demonstrations and showing people what shire horses would have done "back in the day, by pulling agricultural implements, driving wagons", and is now learning to have people ride him. "He's very happy, and he just loves a good fuss," Masters added. Image source, Tove Valley Shire HorsesImage caption, Hugo is much taller than his half-brother, Masters saidDo you have a story suggestion for Northamptonshire? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice
